lesson.title: Not All Static Is Random: Interference from Other Signals
lesson.summary: Interference is unwanted energy from an identifiable transmitter overlapping a receiver's frequency, distinct from random noise, and it is the everyday cost of sharing a broadcast medium like Wi-Fi's crowded 2.4 GHz band.
lesson.body:
Noise, as already described, is essentially random: thermal agitation of electrons, or stray electrical bursts, unpredictable in both timing and shape. Interference is different. It is unwanted energy arriving at a receiver from another identifiable transmitter, one that is sending its own structured signal for its own purposes, and that signal just happens to overlap in frequency, time, or space with the one a receiver is trying to decode. A microwave oven leaking energy into the 2.4 GHz band, a neighbor's Wi-Fi router on an overlapping channel, or two cell towers reusing the same frequency too close together are all sources of interference rather than noise, even though a receiver often cannot easily tell the two apart once they land on the same channel together.

Interference is a particularly sharp problem for the wireless medium precisely because it is shared and broadcast in nature: many independent transmitters can be within range of the same receiver, and none of them are guaranteed to coordinate with each other. Wired links mostly avoid this because each cable is a private, guided path, but a radio has to share open space with every other radio nearby.

Wi-Fi in the 2.4 GHz band offers a concrete, well known example. The band is divided into channels spaced 5 MHz apart, with channel 1 centered at 2412 MHz, channel 6 at 2437 MHz, and channel 11 at 2462 MHz in most regulatory regions. Each Wi-Fi channel actually occupies about 20 to 22 MHz of spectrum, considerably more than the 5 MHz spacing between adjacent channel numbers, which means neighboring channels overlap and interfere with each other. Channels 1 and 6 are 25 MHz apart, and channels 6 and 11 are also 25 MHz apart, just enough separation to keep a 20 to 22 MHz wide channel from overlapping its neighbor. That is why network administrators are told to use only channels 1, 6, and 11 in a crowded building: any other choice, like channel 3 or channel 8, guarantees overlap and mutual interference with whichever of 1, 6, or 11 a nearby network is using.

Interference and noise both lower the effective SNR at the receiver and both increase the chance of a bit being misread, so in practice engineers often lump them together in a single measurement called the noise floor, or the signal to interference plus noise ratio. The distinction still matters for fixing the problem, though: noise from thermal effects cannot be eliminated, only tolerated with a stronger signal or a more robust code, while interference can often be reduced or avoided entirely through channel planning, directional antennas, or scheduling, precisely because it comes from an identifiable, structured source rather than random chance.

Whatever the source, the end result for the receiver is the same: some bits arrive flipped from what was sent. The next concept, bit error rate, is exactly how that outcome gets measured and tracked across a real link.
